title: Flower Planting With No Adjacent
statement:
There are `n` gardens numbered `1` to `n`. Each entry `paths[i] = [x_i, y_i]` is a two-way path joining garden `x_i` and garden `y_i`, and no garden is an endpoint of more than 3 paths.

Plant one flower type in every garden, choosing from the types `1`, `2`, `3` and `4`, so that any two gardens joined by a path hold different types. Return an array `answer` of length `n` where `answer[i]` is the type planted in garden `i + 1`. Such a planting always exists, and any valid planting is accepted.
constraints: Every garden is an endpoint of at most 3 paths
notes:
## Intuition

Coloring a general graph with few colors is hard, and a brute force would backtrack over up to 4^n plantings. Here the degree limit makes it easy: a garden has at most 3 neighbours, so at most 3 of the 4 types are ruled out, and at least one type is always free. That means we can simply go through the gardens one by one and give each the smallest type its already-planted neighbours do not use. No choice ever needs to be undone.

## Approach

1. Build an adjacency list `neighbors` from `paths`, adding each path in both directions.
2. Start with `answer` filled with `0`, meaning "not planted yet".
3. For each `garden` from 1 to `n`, collect the types of its neighbours in `used` (unplanted ones add a harmless `0`).
4. Raise `flower` from 1 until it is not in `used`; this needs at most 4 tries.
5. Store it in `answer[garden - 1]` and return `answer` at the end.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3`, `paths = [[1,2],[2,3],[3,1]]`, so every garden neighbours the other two. Garden 1 sees only unplanted neighbours (`used = {0}`) and gets type 1. Garden 2 sees types 1 and 0, so it gets 2. Garden 3 sees types 2 and 1, so it gets 3. The answer is `[1,2,3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + p) for `p = paths.length`: building the lists touches each path twice, and each garden checks at most 3 neighbours and 4 types.
- Space: O(n + p) for the adjacency lists and `answer`.

## Pitfalls

- Gardens are numbered from 1 but `answer` is indexed from 0: garden `g` lives at `answer[g - 1]`.
- Paths go both ways; adding only `x -> y` lets garden `y` miss a conflict with `x`.
- A BFS or DFS coloring is not needed and can be wrong if it only compares with the parent; check every planted neighbour.
- Several answers are valid, so do not expect your output to match the examples exactly.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `neighbors` | `neighbors[g]` lists the gardens joined to garden `g` |
| `answer` | the flower type of each garden, `0` while unplanted |
| `garden` | the garden being planted |
| `next` | one neighbour of `garden` |
| `used` | types already taken by its neighbours |
| `flower` | the smallest type not in `used` |

narration.2: Make an empty neighbour list for every garden; index 0 is unused because gardens start at 1.
narration.4: A path works both ways, so garden y is a neighbour of x...
narration.5: ...and x is a neighbour of y.
narration.7: 0 marks a garden that has no flower yet.
narration.8: Plant the gardens in order from 1 to n.
narration.9: Collect the types this garden must avoid.
narration.10: Look at each neighbour of this garden.
narration.11: Record its type; an unplanted neighbour adds 0, which never blocks a real type.
narration.14: Skip every type a neighbour already uses; at most 3 types can be blocked...
narration.15: ...so stepping to the next type stops by type 4 at the latest.
narration.17: Plant the free type; garden g is stored at index g - 1.
narration.19: Every garden now differs from all of its neighbours.
